position: both — the 'habitual' sense only before a noun: *a confirmed bachelor*

senses.gloss: Shown or officially stated to be true or definite.
examples: There are now twelve *confirmed* cases in the county.
Your reservation is *confirmed* for Friday at seven.
We have no *confirmed* reports of injuries.

senses.gloss: Firmly fixed in a habit or way of life and unlikely to change.
examples: He's a *confirmed* bachelor who likes living alone.
I'm a *confirmed* night owl, so don't call me before ten.

senses.gloss: Different from each other and impossible to agree or be true at the same time.
examples: We got *conflicting* reports about what happened.
The advice from the two doctors was *conflicting*.
She had *conflicting* feelings about moving away.

senses.gloss: Following the usual rules and behaving the way most people expect.
examples: The school had a very *conformist* culture.
His parents were more *conformist* than he was.
She rejected the *conformist* life of the suburbs.

position: both — the research sense only before a noun: *a confounding variable*

senses.gloss: Confusing and hard to understand or explain.
examples: The disappearance remains one of the most *confounding* mysteries of the decade.
The new tax rules are *confounding* even to accountants.

senses.gloss: In research, affecting the result in a way that hides the real cause.
examples: Age was a *confounding* factor in the study.
The researchers tried to control for *confounding* variables.

senses.gloss: Tending to argue with or challenge people in an aggressive way.
examples: He has a very *confrontational* style of management.
Try not to be so *confrontational* when you talk to her.
The second debate was more *confrontational* than the first.

senses.gloss: Relating to Confucius or the ideas he taught about family, duty and social order.
examples: Respect for elders is a central *Confucian* value.
The book traces *Confucian* influence on Korean society.
Her upbringing was strict and deeply *Confucian*.

senses.gloss: Changed from a liquid into a thick, almost solid state, usually by cooling.
examples: There was *congealed* gravy on the plates.
By morning, the grease in the pan was *congealed*.
He wiped the *congealed* blood from the cut.

takes: *to* + noun — suited to someone's taste or needs
contrast: A false friend: Russian *конгениальный* means 'equal in talent or spirit' (*конгениальный перевод*). English *congenial* just means pleasant and friendly.

senses.gloss: Pleasant and friendly, or suited to your tastes.
examples: Our host was *congenial* and made everyone feel at home.
The office has a *congenial* atmosphere.
She found the small town more *congenial* than the city.

position: both — the 'by nature' sense only before a noun: *a congenital liar*

senses.gloss: Present from birth.
examples: The baby was born with a *congenital* heart defect.
Doctors said the condition was *congenital*.

senses.gloss: Having a bad habit or quality so strongly that it seems part of your nature.
examples: He's a *congenital* liar.
She has a *congenital* inability to be on time.

senses.gloss: So full of traffic or people that movement is difficult.
examples: The freeway is always *congested* at rush hour.
Los Angeles has some of the most *congested* roads in the country.
We avoided the *congested* downtown streets.

senses.gloss: Blocked with mucus, so that breathing is hard.
examples: My nose is so *congested* I can't smell anything.
The medicine helps clear a *congested* chest.

senses.gloss: In medicine, caused by too much blood or fluid collecting in part of the body.
examples: His grandfather died of *congestive* heart failure.
Swollen ankles can be a sign of *congestive* heart failure.
She is being treated for a *congestive* condition.

contrast: It covers both countries, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. It is also the noun for the people, and the plural does not change: *two Congolese*, *the Congolese*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the Congo, its people or its culture.
examples: *Congolese* music is popular all over Africa.
The restaurant is run by a *Congolese* family.
Her husband is *Congolese*.

senses.gloss: Expressing congratulations or praise.
examples: The coach got a *congratulatory* call from the governor.
She received dozens of *congratulatory* messages.
The tone of the email was warm and *congratulatory*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the US Congress.
examples: She's running for a *congressional* seat in Ohio.
The CEO testified at a *congressional* hearing.
Our *congressional* district was redrawn last year.

comparison: not gradable — but *more congruent* in the 'in agreement' sense

senses.gloss: In agreement or fitting well with something.
examples: His actions are not *congruent* with his words.
We want goals that are *congruent* with our values.

senses.gloss: In geometry, having exactly the same size and shape.
examples: The two triangles are *congruent*.
Prove that the angles are *congruent*.

senses.gloss: Shaped like a cone.
examples: The workers wore *conical* straw hats.
The volcano is almost perfectly *conical*.
Pour the batter into a *conical* bag.

senses.gloss: Of trees, having cones and needles that usually stay green all year.
examples: Pines and spruces are *coniferous* trees.
The mountains are covered in *coniferous* forest.
Most of the trees in the park are *coniferous*.

contrast: The usual modern term is *conjoined twins*; the older *Siamese twins* is now avoided.

senses.gloss: Joined together, especially of twins born physically connected.
examples: Surgeons separated the *conjoined* twins in a twelve-hour operation.
The girls were *conjoined* at the hip.
The two buildings are *conjoined* by a glass walkway.

senses.gloss: Relating to marriage or to the relationship between a husband and wife.
examples: Some prisons allow *conjugal* visits.
The couple lived in *conjugal* harmony for fifty years.
The law once gave husbands *conjugal* rights over their wives.

senses.gloss: Related to something else in some way.
examples: Police believe the two robberies are *connected*.
She's had several jobs *connected* with the film industry.
Stress and sleep are closely *connected*.

senses.gloss: Joined physically, or linked to a network such as the internet.
examples: Make sure the printer is *connected* to your laptop.
The kitchen is *connected* to the garage by a short hallway.
Video calls help grandparents stay *connected* with their grandkids.

senses.gloss: Knowing important or powerful people.
examples: Her father is very well *connected* in Washington.
He's one of the most *connected* lobbyists in the state.

senses.gloss: Secretly planning to do something harmful or dishonest.
examples: The show's villain is a *conniving* stepmother.
I didn't realize how *conniving* he could be.
She's the most *conniving* person I've ever worked with.

contrast: Do not confuse with *conscious* (aware, awake). A *conscientious objector* refuses military service on moral grounds.

senses.gloss: Careful to do your work or duty well and thoroughly.
examples: She's the most *conscientious* employee on the team.
He's very *conscientious* about checking his work.
*Conscientious* drivers slow down near schools.

position: both — the 'deliberate' sense mostly before a noun: *a conscious decision*
comparison: more/most — *more conscious*, *most conscious*, in the 'aware' sense
contrast: Russian *сознательный* about a responsible person is not *conscious*: say *responsible* or *socially aware*. *Self-conscious* means shy and embarrassed, not *сознательный*. Do not confuse with *conscientious*.

senses.gloss: Awake and able to see, hear and think.
examples: The driver was *conscious* when the paramedics arrived.
He was barely *conscious* after the fall.

senses.gloss: Knowing about something or noticing it.
examples: I was *conscious* of people staring at me.
People are more *conscious* of their health than they used to be.
She's very *conscious* that time is running out.

senses.gloss: Done on purpose, with full awareness.
examples: We made a *conscious* decision not to have a TV.
It takes a *conscious* effort to slow down.

senses.gloss: Officially made holy in a religious ceremony.
examples: The soldiers are buried in *consecrated* ground.
The bread and wine are *consecrated* during the service.
The priest placed the *consecrated* host on the altar.

contrast: Russian *последовательный* also means 'logical, not changing your views'; that is *consistent*, not *consecutive*. *Consecutive* only means one after another: *three consecutive wins* = *три победы подряд*.

senses.gloss: Following one after another without a break.
examples: It rained for five *consecutive* days.
The team won its third *consecutive* championship.
Make sure the page numbers are *consecutive*.

senses.gloss: Done with the agreement of everyone involved.
examples: Both sides said the relationship was *consensual*.
The officer said the search of the car was *consensual*.
The group prefers a *consensual* approach to decisions.

senses.gloss: Agreeing freely to take part in something.
examples: What *consenting* adults do in private is their own business.
Only *consenting* patients were included in the study.
The law applies to relationships between *consenting* adults.

position: both — the 'resulting' sense only before a noun: *consequential damages*

senses.gloss: Important, with serious effects.
examples: This could be the most *consequential* election of our lifetime.
The decision turned out to be very *consequential*.

senses.gloss: Happening as a result of something else.
examples: The contract does not cover *consequential* damages.
The flood caused a *consequential* loss of business.

contrast: In US politics *conservative* means on the right, usually closer to the Republican Party. A *conservative estimate* is deliberately low, not old-fashioned.

senses.gloss: Holding traditional political or social views and wanting little change.
examples: She grew up in a *conservative* town in Texas.
Rural voters tend to be more *conservative* than city voters.
He writes for a *conservative* magazine.

senses.gloss: Plain and traditional in style, not showy.
examples: Wear a *conservative* suit to the interview.
Her taste in furniture is pretty *conservative*.

senses.gloss: Of a guess or estimate, deliberately low or cautious.
examples: At a *conservative* estimate, the repairs will cost $5,000.
The company's forecast was *conservative*.

contrast: Do not confuse with *considerate* (thoughtful toward others). *A considerable person* is not a thing; say *a considerate person*.

senses.gloss: Fairly large in size, amount or degree.
examples: The project took a *considerable* amount of time.
The storm caused *considerable* damage to the roof.
The cost of moving was *considerable*.

takes: *of* + person (*it was considerate of you*); *to* or *toward* + person
contrast: Do not confuse with *considerable* (large in amount).

senses.gloss: Thinking about other people's feelings and needs.
examples: It was very *considerate* of you to call ahead.
Our neighbors are quiet and *considerate*.
You could be a little more *considerate* toward your sister.

takes: *with* + noun — in agreement with; *in* + noun or *-ing* — steady in

senses.gloss: Always behaving or happening in the same way, or keeping the same quality.
examples: He's the most *consistent* player on the team.
You need to be *consistent* with the rules you set for kids.
The restaurant's food is good and *consistent*.

senses.gloss: In agreement with other facts or ideas.
examples: The injuries are *consistent* with a fall.

senses.gloss: Formed by joining several things into one.

The kids attend a *consolidated* school district.
We paid off our credit cards with a *consolidated* loan.

senses.gloss: Very easy to see or notice.

In his orange jacket, he was more *conspicuous* than he wanted to be.
The mayor was *conspicuous* by his absence.

senses.gloss: Suggesting that people share a secret.
examples: She gave me a *conspiratorial* wink.
He lowered his voice to a *conspiratorial* whisper.

senses.gloss: Relating to a secret plot, or believing that one exists.
examples: The forum is full of *conspiratorial* thinking.
His explanations grew more *conspiratorial* every year.

position: both — the 'loyal' sense only before a noun: *a constant companion*

senses.gloss: Happening all the time or again and again.
examples: I'm tired of the *constant* noise from the construction site.
The baby needs *constant* attention.
Their arguments were *constant*.

senses.gloss: Staying at the same level or rate.
examples: Keep the oven at a *constant* temperature.
The car was moving at a *constant* speed.

senses.gloss: Always there and loyal.
examples: The dog was his *constant* companion.
Her mother was a *constant* source of support.

senses.gloss: Unable to empty your bowels easily.
examples: Drink more water if you're *constipated*.
This medication can make you *constipated*.
The vet said the *constipated* cat needed more fiber.

senses.gloss: Relating to a constitution, or allowed by it.
examples: Free speech is a *constitutional* right.
The Supreme Court will decide whether the law is *constitutional*.
She teaches *constitutional* law at Georgetown.

senses.gloss: Limited by rules, money or circumstances.
examples: Schools are *constrained* by tight budgets.
We're working in a very *constrained* time frame.

senses.gloss: Not natural or relaxed.
examples: He gave a *constrained* smile.
The conversation felt more *constrained* after the argument.

senses.gloss: Too tight, or limiting what you can do.
examples: I can't run in these *constricting* jeans.
She found office life *constricting*.
The old rules were even more *constricting*.

senses.gloss: Helpful and meant to improve things.
examples: Thanks for the *constructive* criticism.
The meeting was short but *constructive*.
Let's find a more *constructive* way to deal with this.

senses.gloss: Relating to a consul or a consulate.
examples: The embassy offers *consular* services to citizens abroad.
He asked to speak to a *consular* officer.
You'll need to schedule a *consular* interview for your visa.

senses.gloss: Giving advice rather than making decisions.
examples: The committee has a purely *consultative* role.
She takes a *consultative* approach with her clients.
The council's function is *consultative*, not legislative.

contrast: The plural noun *consumables* means supplies that get used up, such as ink or paper.

senses.gloss: Meant to be used up and then replaced, or able to be eaten or used.
examples: The budget covers *consumable* supplies like paper and ink.
Filters are *consumable* parts that need replacing.
Only *consumable* items were allowed in the care package.

contrast: The verb *consummate* ends in /eɪt/: KAHN-suh-mayt. The adjective ends in a weak /ət/.

senses.gloss: Extremely skilled; perfect in a particular role.
examples: She's a *consummate* professional.
He played the piece with *consummate* skill.
The senator was a *consummate* politician.

senses.gloss: Of a disease or person, able to pass illness to others by contact.
examples: Measles is one of the most *contagious* diseases.
Stay home while you're still *contagious*.

senses.gloss: Of a feeling or behavior, quickly spreading to other people.
examples: She has a *contagious* laugh.
His enthusiasm was *contagious*.

senses.gloss: Made dirty or harmful by something such as chemicals, bacteria or radiation.
examples: Residents were told not to drink the *contaminated* water.
The lettuce was *contaminated* with E. coli.
It's one of the most *contaminated* sites in the country.

senses.gloss: Quiet and thoughtful, or spent in deep thought or prayer.
examples: He was in a *contemplative* mood after the funeral.
The monks lead a *contemplative* life.
Her later paintings are quieter and more *contemplative*.

senses.gloss: Existing or happening at the same time as something else.
examples: The detective relied on *contemporaneous* notes.
The two civilizations were roughly *contemporaneous*.
His career was *contemporaneous* with the rise of television.

comparison: not gradable — but *more contemporary* of style and design
contrast: *Contemporary* can mean 'of today' or 'of that time': *contemporary accounts of the Civil War* were written during the war, not recently.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the present time; modern.
examples: The museum focuses on *contemporary* art.
The house has a clean, *contemporary* design.
Her music is very *contemporary*.

senses.gloss: Living or happening at the same time as a particular person or event in the past.
examples: *Contemporary* newspapers described the fire in detail.
Shakespeare was *contemporary* with Cervantes.

contrast: *Contemptible* describes what deserves contempt; *contemptuous* describes the person who feels it. *His lie was contemptible; she was contemptuous of him.*

senses.gloss: So bad or dishonest that it deserves no respect.
examples: Stealing from a charity is *contemptible*.
It was the most *contemptible* thing he'd ever done.
She called the ad a *contemptible* lie.

contrast: *Contemptuous* is the person or look that shows contempt; *contemptible* is what deserves it.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something is worthless.
examples: She gave him a *contemptuous* look.
He was openly *contemptuous* of the new rules.
The critics were even more *contemptuous* of the sequel.

contrast: *Content* means the same but normally comes only after a verb (*I'm content*); *contented* also goes before a noun (*a contented sigh*).

senses.gloss: Happy and satisfied with what you have.
examples: The baby gave a *contented* sigh and fell asleep.
They seem *contented* with their quiet life.
I've never seen him more *contented*.

senses.gloss: Likely to cause disagreement.
examples: Immigration remains a *contentious* issue.
The new stadium plan is highly *contentious*.

senses.gloss: Full of arguments, or tending to argue.
examples: They went through a long, *contentious* divorce.
It was the most *contentious* board meeting in years.

senses.gloss: Argued about, or competed for by two or more sides.
examples: It was one of the most hotly *contested* elections in state history.
The region is still *contested* territory.
The facts of the case are not *contested*.

senses.gloss: Relating to or depending on the situation something is in.
examples: Use *contextual* clues to guess the meaning of a new word.
The ads are based on *contextual* information.
Whether the joke is offensive is partly *contextual*.

contrast: *The contiguous United States* means the 48 states that border each other, without Alaska and Hawaii.

senses.gloss: Touching or next to each other, with no gap.
examples: Shipping is free within the *contiguous* United States.
The two properties are *contiguous*.
The park is *contiguous* with a national forest.

contrast: A *continental breakfast* at an American hotel is a light one: bread, pastries, coffee and juice, with no hot food.

senses.gloss: Relating to a continent, or to the main land of a continent.
examples: The offer is valid in the *continental* United States.
The region has a *continental* climate, with hot summers and cold winters.

senses.gloss: Relating to mainland Europe, especially in style.
examples: The hotel serves a free *continental* breakfast.
The restaurant has a *continental* menu.

position: both — the 'depending' sense after a verb, the 'temporary' sense before a noun
contrast: The noun *a contingent* is a group of people (*a large Canadian contingent*), close to Russian *контингент* in the sense of a group sent somewhere.

senses.gloss: Depending on something else happening.
examples: The job offer is *contingent* on a background check.
Our plans are *contingent* upon the weather.

senses.gloss: Of workers, hired only for a limited time or for particular tasks.
examples: Many colleges rely on *contingent* faculty.
*Contingent* workers often get no health benefits.

contrast: After a verb it is the verb: *To be continued*, *The story is continued on page 6*.

senses.gloss: Going on without stopping, or happening again.
examples: Thank you for your *continued* support.
The *continued* rain caused flooding downtown.
His *continued* absence worried his boss.

senses.gloss: Still happening or existing.
examples: The town is dealing with a *continuing* water shortage.
Nurses must take *continuing* education courses.
It's a *continuing* problem for small businesses.

senses.gloss: Twisted out of its normal shape, or too complicated to follow easily.
examples: His face was *contorted* with pain.
The yoga teacher held a *contorted* pose.
The lawyer's arguments grew more *contorted* as the trial went on.

contrast: It is also a noun: *a contraceptive* is a pill or device that prevents pregnancy.

senses.gloss: Used to prevent a woman from becoming pregnant.
examples: The clinic offers free *contraceptive* pills.
Her insurance covers most *contraceptive* methods.
The study looked at *contraceptive* use among college students.

senses.gloss: Stated in or required by a contract.
examples: The company has a *contractual* obligation to finish by June.
He's in a *contractual* dispute with his record label.
The bonus is *contractual*, so they have to pay it.

contrast: *Contradictory* means the parts say opposite things. For a *противоречивый* person or film that people argue about, say *controversial*.

senses.gloss: Containing ideas or statements that cannot all be true.
examples: The witnesses gave *contradictory* accounts.
The instructions are confusing and *contradictory*.
His second statement was even more *contradictory* than the first.

comparison: not gradable — but *more contrary* in the 'stubborn' sense
contrast: *On the contrary* is a fixed phrase that rejects what was just said. In the 'stubborn' sense some speakers stress the second syllable: kuhn-TRER-ee.

senses.gloss: Completely different or opposite.
examples: Some experts hold the *contrary* view.
*Contrary* to popular belief, bats aren't blind.
The results were *contrary* to what we expected.

senses.gloss: Deliberately doing or saying the opposite of what others want.
examples: He's being *contrary* just to annoy you.
My toddler is at a very *contrary* age.

senses.gloss: Very different from each other in a noticeable way.
examples: The jacket has *contrasting* stitching.
The two candidates offered sharply *contrasting* visions.
Paint the trim a *contrasting* color.

senses.gloss: Helping to cause something.
examples: Fatigue was a *contributing* factor in the crash.
Stress can be a *contributing* cause of heart disease.

senses.gloss: Writing for a magazine or newspaper regularly without being on its staff.
examples: She's a *contributing* editor at a travel magazine.
He became a *contributing* writer for the sports section.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing sorrow for something wrong you have done.
examples: He gave a *contrite* apology.
The senator looked *contrite* as he spoke to reporters.
She seemed more *contrite* the second time.

senses.gloss: Obviously planned or invented, and not natural or believable.
examples: The movie's ending felt *contrived*.
It was a *contrived* excuse to see her again.
The dialogue gets more *contrived* in the second season.

senses.gloss: Able to be controlled or managed.
examples: Focus on the *controllable* parts of the problem.
With medication, her symptoms are *controllable*.
The new drone is lighter and more *controllable*.

position: both — the 'regulated' sense mostly before a noun: *a controlled substance*
comparison: more/most — *more controlled*, *most controlled*, in the 'calm' sense

senses.gloss: Calm and not showing strong emotion.
examples: She spoke in a slow, *controlled* voice.
His second performance was more *controlled*.

senses.gloss: Limited or regulated by rules or laws, or carefully managed.
examples: He was arrested for possession of a *controlled* substance.
The fire department started a *controlled* burn.
The scientists ran a *controlled* experiment.

position: both — the 'ownership' sense only before a noun: *a controlling interest*
comparison: more/most — *more controlling*, *most controlling*, in the 'bossy' sense

senses.gloss: Trying too hard to control other people's lives.
examples: Her ex-boyfriend was jealous and *controlling*.

senses.gloss: Having the power to make decisions for a company or group.
examples: The family still owns a *controlling* interest in the company.

contrast: For statements that contradict each other, use *contradictory*, not *controversial*. *Controversial* means that people argue about it.

senses.gloss: Causing a lot of public disagreement.
examples: The decision to close the school was very *controversial*.
She's one of the most *controversial* figures in Hollywood.

takes: *for* + person or purpose; *to* + place — close to

senses.gloss: Easy to use or suitable for your plans, so that it saves time or trouble.

senses.gloss: Near and easy to get to.

position: both — the 'non-nuclear' sense only before a noun: *conventional weapons*

senses.gloss: Of weapons or war, not nuclear.

contrast: Do not confuse with *conversational* (informal, like talk). In American use *conversant in Spanish* means you can hold a conversation in it.

senses.gloss: Informal and like ordinary talk, or used in conversation.

contrast: The noun *a convertible* is a car with a roof that folds down (*кабриолет*).

senses.gloss: Of money or investments, able to be exchanged for something else.

senses.gloss: Curving outward, like the outside of a ball.

contrast: The *-ed* form is the person who believes (*I'm convinced*); the *-ing* form is what makes you believe (*a convincing argument*).

senses.gloss: Friendly, cheerful and good for enjoying company.

senses.gloss: Heated and prepared so that it is ready to eat.

senses.gloss: Made to the same pattern as many others, with nothing original about it.

I'm tired of *cookie-cutter* superhero movies.
We don't offer *cookie-cutter* solutions.

contrast: *Cool* is not as cold as *cold*: *прохладный*, not *холодный*. In the 'great' sense it is very informal.

senses.gloss: Slightly cold, often in a pleasant way.
examples: It's *cooler* in the mountains.
Store the potatoes in a *cool*, dry place.
The evening air was *cool*.

senses.gloss: Calm and not nervous or excited.
examples: She stayed *cool* under pressure.
He kept a *cool* head during the emergency.

senses.gloss: Informal: fashionable, attractive or very good.
examples: That's a really *cool* jacket.
He thinks he's the *coolest* guy in school.
Your new place is so *cool*.

senses.gloss: Informal: fine, acceptable, or not upset.
examples: I'm *cool* with ordering pizza.
Sorry about last night. Are we *cool*?

senses.gloss: Unfriendly or not enthusiastic.
examples: The plan got a *cool* reception from voters.
She was polite but *cool* toward me.

position: both — the 'owned by members' sense only before a noun
contrast: The noun *a cooperative* or *a co-op* is a business or apartment building owned by its members.

senses.gloss: Willing to help or do what people ask.
examples: The witness was very *cooperative* with police.
The kids were more *cooperative* after lunch.

senses.gloss: Done by people working together.
examples: The project was a *cooperative* effort between two schools.
*Cooperative* games teach kids teamwork.

senses.gloss: Owned and run by the people who use it or work in it.
examples: We buy our vegetables at a *cooperative* grocery store.
The farmers formed a *cooperative* dairy.

senses.gloss: Organized so that different people or parts work together.
examples: Police said it was a *coordinated* attack.
We need a more *coordinated* response to the crisis.

senses.gloss: Able to control your body's movements well.
examples: I'm not *coordinated* enough to dance.
She's the most *coordinated* kid on the soccer team.

senses.gloss: Of clothes or colors, chosen to look good together.
examples: The bridesmaids wore *coordinated* dresses.
Their outfits were perfectly *coordinated*.

contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned or jokey. Also spelled *copacetic*.

senses.gloss: Informal: fine, satisfactory, with no problems.
examples: Don't worry, everything's *copasetic*.
Things between us are *copasetic* now.
As long as the rent gets paid, we're *copasetic*.

senses.gloss: Large in amount; plentiful.
examples: She took *copious* notes during the lecture.
The recipe calls for *copious* amounts of garlic.
The rainfall this spring was more *copious* than usual.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Copts, the Christian community of Egypt, or their church or language.
examples: The *Coptic* Orthodox Church is one of the oldest in the world.
They visited a *Coptic* monastery near Cairo.
The manuscript is written in *Coptic* script.

senses.gloss: Legally protected so that others may not copy or use it without permission.
examples: You can't post *copyrighted* music without permission.
All photos on this site are *copyrighted*.
The video was removed for using *copyrighted* material.

senses.gloss: Behaving in a playful way to attract romantic attention.
examples: She gave him a *coquettish* smile.
Her tone was light and *coquettish*.
The character is more *coquettish* in the movie than in the book.

contrast: Only the color is an adjective. In *a coral reef* or *coral jewelry*, *coral* is a noun used as a modifier.

senses.gloss: Pinkish orange in color.
examples: She wore a *coral* dress to the wedding.
The walls are painted a soft *coral* shade.
Her lipstick was bright *coral*.

contrast: *Cordial* is often weaker than Russian *сердечный*: *cordial relations* are polite and friendly, not necessarily warm. The noun *a cordial* is a sweet liqueur.

senses.gloss: Friendly and polite, often in a formal way.
examples: The two leaders had a *cordial* meeting.
Relations with our neighbors are *cordial* but not close.
She was more *cordial* to me than I expected.

senses.gloss: Working on a battery, without an electric cord.
examples: I bought a *cordless* drill.
Our old home phone was *cordless*.
*Cordless* vacuums are easier to carry upstairs.

senses.gloss: Of animals, fed on corn.
examples: The restaurant serves *corn-fed* beef.
Most chicken in the store is *corn-fed*.

senses.gloss: Informal: healthy, simple and typical of the rural Midwest.
examples: He's a big, *corn-fed* farm boy from Iowa.
The ad was full of *corn-fed* small-town values.

senses.gloss: Trapped, with no easy way to escape or get out of a situation.
examples: A *cornered* animal can be dangerous.
He felt *cornered* by the reporters' questions.
When she's *cornered*, she gets defensive.

senses.gloss: Too familiar, silly or sentimental to be taken seriously.
examples: My dad loves telling *corny* jokes.
I know it sounds *corny*, but you changed my life.
That's the *corniest* love song I've ever heard.

contrast: The noun *a coronary* is an informal word for a heart attack: *He almost had a coronary when he saw the bill.*

senses.gloss: Relating to the arteries that carry blood to the heart.
examples: *Coronary* heart disease is a leading cause of death.
The surgeon found a blockage in a *coronary* artery.
He was taken straight to the *coronary* care unit.
